tier_reason: goja's own README gives only an unsupported '6-7 times faster than otto' sentence, which on its own is tier C. The Tengo README benchmark table is an independent third-party measurement with public code (d5/tengobench, whose go.mod pins goja 2020-04-14 and otto 2019-12-19). It shows fib(35) goja 5,194 ms vs otto 48,539 ms, but it states no hardware or Go toolchain, so B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: goja README: 'it's 6-7 times faster than otto on average'. No workload, code or numbers are given; the linked issue #2 holds only a user's question asking for them. The independent Tengo README table (code in d5/tengobench) gives fib(35): goja 5,194 ms vs otto 48,539 ms, about 9.3x (derived from page data). It also gives fibt(35): goja 4 ms vs otto 6 ms. In the same table goja is slower than Tengo (2,315 ms), go-lua (4,028 ms) and GopherLua (4,409 ms), and native CPython 2 runs fib(35) in 1,907 ms.
corrections.workload: Tengo table: recursive fib(35) and tail-call fibt(35), one run each, script read from file (tengobench code/ directory). The README's '6-7 times on average' has no stated workload.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: tengobench go.mod: go 1.14 directive; goja v0.0.0-20200414142002-77e84ffb8c65, otto v0.0.0-20191219234010-c382bd3c16ff. The Go toolchain and flags used for the published table are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The README ratio has no workload, hardware or method. Issue goja#2, which the README links as 'some benchmarks', was opened on 2016-11-11 by a user (mbertschler) asking for the benchmark code and results. It is still open, with no maintainer reply and no numbers. The independent evidence is one 2020-era micro-benchmark (fib(35)) from a competitor's README, with no hardware and no repeated runs. The baseline otto is a slow tree-walking interpreter. goja does not beat V8, QuickJS or any engine in the category baseline list, and its own README says it is not a replacement for V8 or SpiderMonkey. The LICENSE is MIT, with copyrights for both Dmitry Panov and Robert Krimen (otto's author).

notes: Upgraded C to B on the independent Tengo/tengobench fib(35) numbers. The record's caveat that 'the maintainer's comment holds only the same sentence' was wrong: issue #2 was a user's question that the maintainer never answered. Metadata checks out: MIT, 7.1k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived. As a Go-embedded JS engine, the better-fitting category is wave 12's embedded-scripting. Fork maclof/goja-perf is a separate merged entry that benchmarks against upstream goja.

tier_reason: The first-party wiki page (last edited 2016-08-20 by the author) shows the fib(35) source for every implementation, plus Go 1.7, Lua 5.1.4, Python 3.4.3 and 'Windows7 64bit CPU:2, Memory:8GB'. It names no CPU model and no build flags, and each implementation was timed once, so it is not A; the numbers are first-party, so C.

corrections.caveats: This is a 2016 single-benchmark wiki page (Go 1.7, Python 3.4.3, Windows 7, no CPU model, one run each), and the margin over CPython is about 8%. GopherLua is about 3.2x slower than reference C Lua 5.1.4 on the same page. The CPython comparison is obsolete: CPython 3.11+ is much faster than 3.4. The independent Tengo README table (d5/tengobench, gopher-lua pinned 2019-12-20) contradicts the claim: there GopherLua takes 4,409 ms for fib(35) against 1,907 ms for native CPython 2, so CPython is about 2.3x faster (derived from page data). The wins are really over other Go-hosted interpreters (go-lua, otto, anko), which are not category baselines. Included mainly as the reference for Go-hosted Lua VMs.

notes: The numbers match the wiki page exactly (GopherLua 5.40 s, Python3.4 5.84 s, lua5.1.4 1.71 s, go-lua 8.13 s, otto 173.32 s, anko 182.73 s). Metadata checks out: MIT, about 7.0k stars, last commit 2026-04-01, active (the README was converted from rst to md that day). Main shortcomings: the claimed win over CPython is marginal and obsolete, and it is contradicted by an independent run. As a Go-embedded Lua VM, the better-fitting category is wave 12's embedded-scripting.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party speedups against CPython 3.7, and the benchmark scripts are public in src/benchmarks/ (richards.py, raytrace.py, unpack_sequence_fast.py, unpack_sequence_slow.py). The Dockerfile names clang 13, but the headline 9.5x and 3-4.5x numbers come from unnamed 'internal dev machines' with no CPU model, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Public Dockerfile: clang 13 (apt.llvm.org); CPython 3.7 branch built from source with CFLAGS=-fno-omit-frame-pointer and ./configure --enable-shared (no --enable-optimizations/PGO). The build behind the internal-machine numbers is not stated.
corrections.workload: Three pyperformance benchmarks modified by DeepMind, in src/benchmarks/: richards.py, raytrace.py, and unpack_sequence_fast.py / unpack_sequence_slow.py. pyperf was removed because it segfaults under S6. Each script runs the plain CPython 3.7 interpreter, then the @s6.jit version, in the same process.
corrections.caveats: The repo was archived on 2023-07-05 and holds one Copybara import commit (2022-09-14); DeepMind says it stopped work on S6. The README says most testing used internal or private benchmarks; the public numbers are for three modified pyperformance benchmarks on unnamed hardware. The harness (e.g. src/benchmarks/richards.py) times one wall-clock run of each mode with time.time(), with no repetitions. It ignores the benchmark's own correctness return value, so a wrong-result run would still print a speedup. The S6 timing includes JIT warm-up. The public Dockerfile's baseline CPython is a non-PGO build with frame pointers kept, which is slower than a distribution CPython. On unpack_sequence S6 is 5x slower (0.2x), or 0.97x in the tweaked variant. Only CPython 3.7 is supported, and it is long out of support. Apache-2.0 is in src/LICENSE and in per-file headers (the root build.sh carries the same header); there is no root LICENSE file.

notes: The claimed speedups match the README (7x Richards at 100 iterations 'depending on your hardware', 9.5x on internal machines, raytrace 3-4.5x, unpack_sequence 0.2x/0.97x, 'up to 10x'). Last commit corrected from null to 2022-09-14. Main shortcomings: archived, CPython 3.7 only, a single-run harness that does not check results, and no hardware named. The real category is wave 12's jits (it is a JIT for CPython), not language-interpreters.
